metaDescription: Hold mineral rights near Theodore, AL, in the Mobile County Gulf Coast oil corridor? We check activity near the Hatters Pond trend and make a cash offer.
heroLead: Theodore sits in the industrial belt south of Mobile, inside a county where salt-structure gas fields and Gulf Coast oil history shape what a mineral interest is worth.
intro: Theodore grew up as an unincorporated crossroads community south of Mobile, and today it's better known for the Alabama State Docks industrial corridor than for oil derricks. But the mineral estate under and around Theodore sits inside Mobile County's Gulf Coast play, where Norphlet gas and Smackover-trend oil have supported production at fields like Hatters Pond for decades. A lot of families in the area hold an interest that was severed generations ago and has quietly collected small royalty checks, or none at all, since.

We look at where your parcel falls relative to the county's producing units before we say anything about value, because a Theodore tract near an active salt-structure gas field prices very differently than one several miles off the trend.

sections.heading: The salt-structure gas trend near Theodore
paragraphs: Mobile County's most productive gas fields, including Hatters Pond, sit over deep salt-related structures that trap Norphlet sandstone gas and Smackover oil beneath a caprock. Theodore itself is close enough to this structural trend that some parcels in the area have historic leasing or unitization history even without a well on the specific tract, because operators held large blocks together under a single unit.

If your deed references a unit rather than a single well, that's normal for this part of the county, and it usually means your royalty, if any, is calculated on a proportional share of everything the unit produces.

sections.heading: Industrial surface use, split mineral ownership
paragraphs: Because Theodore's surface has been used for shipbuilding, chemical plants, and port-adjacent industry for decades, it's common here for the surface owner and the mineral owner to be entirely different people, sometimes with no connection to each other at all. That split can make paperwork feel more complicated than it is. What matters to us is your chain of title in the mineral estate, not who owns or operates the surface today.

We also see a fair number of Theodore interests tied up in old family land that was subdivided for industrial development decades ago, with the mineral rights carved out and retained by a prior owner. If that sounds like your situation, we can usually trace it from the Mobile County Probate Court records.

sections.heading: Building a fair number for Theodore acreage
paragraphs: For producing interest, we weigh recent royalty statements against how the field has historically declined, since Norphlet gas wells in this part of the Gulf Coast trend can hold a plateau for years before tapering. For non-producing acreage, pricing depends heavily on proximity to the active structural trend and whether there's been recent leasing interest nearby, and we'll walk you through exactly how we got to our number rather than just handing you a figure.
We never promise a specific dollar-per-acre outcome up front. What we can promise is a written offer with the reasoning behind it, so you can compare it against anything else you're considering.

faqs.question: Is my Theodore mineral interest connected to the Hatters Pond field?
faqs.answer: Possibly, depending on your exact legal description. We check your parcel against Mobile County unit boundaries and historic field maps before we say how close you are to active salt-structure production.

faqs.question: I only have an old royalty check stub, not a deed. Is that enough to start?
faqs.answer: It's a good start. A royalty statement usually has an operator name and property or unit number we can use to look up your interest in county and state records.

faqs.question: Does industrial development on the surface affect what my mineral rights are worth?
faqs.answer: Generally no, since mineral value is driven by subsurface geology and production history, not surface land use, though it can occasionally affect access for future drilling.
